pi.name: Ming Li
pi.title: Associate Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology; Associate Chair for Research and Facilities
pi.bio: Ming Li grew up in Jingdezhen, China, and was the first in his family to attend college. He earned a B.S. from Fudan University in Shanghai and a Ph.D. from the University of Massachusetts-Amherst, followed by postdoctoral training at UMass-Amherst and Cornell University. He is an Associate Professor in MCDB at the University of Michigan, where he also serves as Associate Chair for Research and Facilities. His lab studies lysosomal membrane protein quality control and lysosome biogenesis in the context of neurodegeneration, cancer, and lysosomal storage diseases; he received an NIH R35 award in 2024.

description: The Ming Li Lab investigates the lysosome: how it is born (biogenesis), how it is regulated to stay functional (quality control), and how it communicates with other organelles. The lab discovered that damaged or misregulated lysosomal membrane proteins are ubiquitinated and internalized by the ESCRT machinery into the lumen for degradation, and it has identified E3 ligase complexes responsible for substrate recognition in yeast and human cells. Through CRISPR screening the lab identified TMEM251 (LYSET) as a Golgi protein essential for the mannose-6-phosphate pathway, whose mutation causes a severe skeletal dysplasia (mucolipidosis type V). Other projects examine ER-associated degradation of mutant cystinosin in cystinosis, where chemical chaperones partially rescue folding and reduce cystine accumulation by about 70 percent, and how cancer cells upregulate lysosome numbers to support rapid growth. The lab uses budding yeast, human cancer cell lines, and vertebrate models including zebrafish and mice.

areas.title: Lysosome membrane quality control via ubiquitin and ESCRT-dependent microautophagy
areas.summary: Studies how damaged or mutated lysosomal membrane proteins are recognized by E3 ligases, ubiquitinated, and internalized by ESCRT machinery for degradation, from yeast vacuoles to human lysosomes, including reconstitution of lysosomal transporters such as Ypq1.

areas.title: TMEM251 and mucolipidosis type V
areas.summary: Characterizes TMEM251, a small Golgi membrane protein identified by CRISPR screening that regulates the M6P pathway for lysosomal enzyme trafficking; current work examines TMEM251-GNPT interactions and zebrafish knockout models.

areas.title: ERAD in cystinosis pathogenesis
areas.summary: Examines how cystinosin mutations cause misfolding and ER-associated degradation, leading to cystine accumulation and kidney and eye damage; chemical chaperones partially rescue the mutant, and the lab is developing mouse models and screening other unstable variants.

areas.title: Lysosome biogenesis in cancer
areas.summary: Explores how cancer cells dramatically increase lysosome numbers to meet nutrient demands, using genome-wide CRISPR screening and live-cell imaging.

joining: Two postdoctoral research associate positions are open to study lysosomal membrane quality control using yeast and mammalian cell lines; applicants need a strong background in molecular and cell biology and published first-author papers, and should email a statement of interest, CV, and three referee contacts to Dr. Ming Li. Graduate students must be enrolled in MCDB or PIBS and can email Dr. Li to arrange a rotation. The lab actively recruits undergraduates, many of whom have become publication co-authors; email Dr. Li for details.
